latest.summary: Brent crude heads towards $103 a barrel while Asian shares slide Tesco shares have gained 2.5% in early London trading, making it one of the top risers on the FTSE 100 index. The wider index is down 0.7%, or 76 points, at 10,381. Tesco has turned in another solid set of results, showing it can keep growing even when the wider economy feels uncertain. Sales, profits, and cash generation are all moving in the right direction, and record customer satisfaction suggests shoppers are responding to its mix of low prices, better quality, and easier ways to shop. Bigger picture, the company’s growth has quietly become a technology story. Clubcard is one of the richest customer datasets in the UK and its retail media business is now using that to sell very effectively to suppliers. On the consumer side, more personalised offers, wider rewards, and tools like the new AI meal planner seem to be landing well with shoppers, helping Tesco deepen relationships and keep customers choosing it over rivals. Sports.title: Is Fury v Joshua about meritocratic sporting excellence or just algorithmic celebrity power? | Jonathan Liew
Sports.summary: This long-awaited fight is happening exactly as intended: at the sweet spot where commercial potential meets a genuine absence of jeopardy The 1912 Olympic marathon was held in a brutal Scandinavian heatwave, and before long Shizo Kanakuri of Japan was flagging. His journey to Stockholm had been debilitating; he had barely trained and struggled to sleep. At around the 16-mile mark he finally gave in. Exhausted and disoriented, he stumbled off the road and into a garden party, where – according to his bemused hosts – he sat and drank orange juice for an hour. The next day, deeply ashamed at his failure to complete the race, he quietly took a boat back to Japan. In Sweden the mystery of the “disappearing runner” took on almost mythical proportions. Kanakuri’s name was on the country’s missing persons list for more than 50 years. Continue reading...

Sports.title: ‘Those memories are ours and no verdict changes that’: Manchester City fans’ views
Sports.summary: While most supporters seem to want to get behind the club, some fear actions of the owners will divide fanbase Nicola Schofield, City fan for more than 40 years: One of my (million) concerns, as someone who feels angry with the owners, is if the owners’ strategy causes a split in the fanbase. I think everyone wants to get behind the club and team, but this is different to the experience of a relegation of the type I experienced in the 90s. We all shared that, and we stood by the club down to League One and as we came back up. This threatens to be messier, with those who may want the owners out (which is its own minefield) to those who will back them all the way. I think ultimately all fans want to ensure our club still exists, but I do worry at divisions this could cause and that might be hard to heal. Ben, season-ticket holder: I don’t think I have fully processed the news yet. I trusted the club completely and believed every word they said in response to the charges, so this has hit hard. I still think the FFP [financial fair play] rules aren’t fair and never have been. I know that won’t get much sympathy from other fans, and I understand why. Most of them have been waiting for this day for years. Whatever happens, nobody can take the last 15 years away from us. We lived every moment: Agüero in 2012, the centurions, the treble, Istanbul. Those memories are ours and no verdict changes that. Right now I just feel confused. One thing won’t change, though: whatever happens, I’ll still support the team. This is character-building, as my parents used to say to me. Continue reading...
